nodes.title: Word, line and character counts
nodes.body:
## Destination

`tally` reports a file's words, lines and characters, each as its own subcommand, and all three at once with `tally all`. Every question that depends on is decided, so the result goes straight to `/to-spec`.

## Notes

- Domain: read `GLOSSARY.md` first. Plain Node.js, no dependencies; tests through `npm test`.
- The existing seam is `run(argv)` in the CLI module, which returns `{ code, out }` without touching the process: test there.

## Decisions so far

- [What is a line?](https://github.com/dbarjs/flow-walk-throwaway/issues/2): a line is a run of characters ended by `\n`, plus a last run with no `\n` if it is non-empty; an empty file has 0 lines; `\r\n` counts once.
- [What is a character?](https://github.com/dbarjs/flow-walk-throwaway/issues/3): a Unicode code point, not a UTF-16 unit and not a byte; `"héllo 👋"` is 7 characters.
- [What does `tally all` print?](https://github.com/dbarjs/flow-walk-throwaway/issues/4): one report of three counts, in the order words, lines, characters, through the existing report formatter; the subcommands `words`, `lines` and `characters` each print a one-count report.

## Not yet specified

Nothing: every decision is made.

## Out of scope

- Reading from standard input, several files at once, and bytes as a count.

nodes.body:
## Question

What does `tally all <file>` print, and how do the single-count subcommands relate to it?

## Answer

One report of three counts, in the order words, lines, characters, through the existing report formatter. The subcommands `words`, `lines` and `characters` each print a one-count report named after the subcommand. Words follow the glossary.

nodes.title: Sentence and paragraph counts
nodes.body:
## Destination

`tally` reports a file's sentences and paragraphs, each as its own subcommand, and both at once with `tally structure`. Every question that depends on is decided, so the result goes straight to `/to-spec`.

## Notes

- Domain: read `GLOSSARY.md` first. Plain Node.js, no dependencies; tests through `npm test`.
- The existing seam is `run(argv)` in the CLI module, which returns `{ code, out }` without touching the process: test there.

## Decisions so far

- [What is a sentence?](https://github.com/dbarjs/flow-walk-throwaway/issues/6): a run of text ended by `.`, `!` or `?`, where several of them in a row end it once, plus a last run with no ending if it holds a word; an empty file has 0 sentences.
- [What is a paragraph?](https://github.com/dbarjs/flow-walk-throwaway/issues/7): one or more lines in a row that are not blank; a line with only whitespace is blank; an empty file has 0 paragraphs.
- [What does `tally structure` print?](https://github.com/dbarjs/flow-walk-throwaway/issues/8): one report of two counts, in the order sentences, paragraphs, through the existing report formatter; the subcommands `sentences` and `paragraphs` each print a one-count report.

## Not yet specified

Nothing: every decision is made.

## Out of scope

- Reading from standard input, several files at once, and abbreviations such as "e.g." (each full stop ends a sentence).

nodes.title: What is a sentence?
nodes.body:
## Question

What does `tally sentences` count as a sentence?

## Answer

A sentence is a run of text ended by `.`, `!` or `?`. Several of them in a row end it once, so `"What?!"` is 1 sentence. A last run with no ending counts if it holds a word. An empty file has 0 sentences. `"Hi! How are you?? Fine"` has 3 sentences. Abbreviations are not special: `"e.g. this"` has 3.

nodes.title: What is a paragraph?
nodes.body:
## Question

What does `tally paragraphs` count as a paragraph?

## Answer

A paragraph is one or more lines in a row that are not blank. A line that holds only whitespace is blank. Any number of blank lines between two paragraphs separates them once. An empty file, or a file of blank lines only, has 0 paragraphs. `"a
b


c"` has 2 paragraphs.

nodes.title: Spec: sentence and paragraph counts (`sentences`, `paragraphs`, `structure`)
nodes.body:
## Problem Statement

`tally` reports counts about a text file, but it cannot say anything about how the file's prose is built. Someone who wants to know how many sentences or paragraphs a draft holds has no subcommand to ask: `tally sentences notes.txt` and `tally paragraphs notes.txt` both print the usage line and exit 2. There is also no way to get both numbers in one report.

## Solution

Three new subcommands, each taking one file:

- `tally sentences <file>` prints a one-count report: `sentences: <number>`.
- `tally paragraphs <file>` prints a one-count report: `paragraphs: <number>`.
- `tally structure <file>` prints one report holding both counts, sentences first.

For a file holding `Hi! How are you??`, a blank line, then `Fine`:

```
$ tally sentences notes.txt
sentences: 3
$ tally paragraphs notes.txt
paragraphs: 2
$ tally structure notes.txt
sentences: 3
paragraphs: 2
```

A **sentence** is a run of text ended by `.`, `!` or `?`. Several of them in a row end it once. A last run with no ending is also a sentence if it holds a word.

A **paragraph** is one or more lines in a row that are not blank. A line that holds only whitespace is blank.

An empty file has 0 sentences and 0 paragraphs.

## User Stories

1. As a writer, I want `tally sentences <file>` to print how many sentences my file holds, so that I can measure a draft in sentences.
2. As a writer, I want `tally paragraphs <file>` to print how many paragraphs my file holds, so that I can measure a draft in paragraphs.
3. As a writer, I want `tally structure <file>` to print both counts in one report, so that I do not have to run `tally` twice.
4. As a writer, I want text ended by `.`, `!` or `?` to count as one sentence, so that statements, exclamations and questions all count.
5. As a writer, I want several ending marks in a row, as in `What?!` or `Wait...`, to end a sentence once, so that emphasis does not inflate the count.
6. As a writer, I want my last sentence to count even before I have typed its full stop, so that a draft in progress is not undercounted.
7. As a writer, I want a line break or trailing spaces after my last full stop not to count as another sentence, so that a file saved with a final newline counts the same as one without.
8. As a writer, I want a sentence that wraps over several lines to count once, so that hard-wrapped text counts the same as unwrapped text.
9. As a writer, I want an empty file to report `sentences: 0`, so that a new file gives a sensible answer and not an error.
10. As a writer, I want a file of only whitespace to report `sentences: 0`, so that stray blank lines are not mistaken for prose.
11. As a writer, I want one fixed rule for full stops (each one ends a sentence, abbreviations included), so that I can explain any count by looking at the text.
12. As a writer, I want several lines in a row with no blank line between them to count as one paragraph, so that hard-wrapped paragraphs count once.
13. As a writer, I want any number of blank lines between two paragraphs to separate them once, so that extra spacing does not create paragraphs.
14. As a writer, I want a line holding only spaces or tabs to count as blank, so that whitespace I cannot see does not join two paragraphs into one.
15. As a writer, I want blank lines at the start or the end of the file not to add paragraphs, so that padding around the text does not change the count.
16. As a writer, I want an empty file, or a file of blank lines only, to report `paragraphs: 0`, so that a file with no text has no paragraphs.
17. As a writer on Windows, I want a file with `\r\n` line endings to give the same paragraph count as the same text with `\n` endings, so that the count does not depend on my editor.
18. As a writer, I want the structure report to list sentences first and paragraphs second every time, so that I always know where to look.
19. As a script author, I want every count printed on its own line as `<name>: <number>`, so that I can parse these reports the same way as any other `tally` report.
20. As a script author, I want a one-count report to carry the name of the subcommand I ran, so that the output names match what I typed.
21. As a script author, I want `tally structure` to print the same numbers that `tally sentences` and `tally paragraphs` print for the same file, so that I can use either form.
22. As a script author, I want exit code 0 whenever a report is printed, so that I can detect success.
23. As a script author, I want each new subcommand to print the usage line and exit 2 when I leave out the file, so that a mistake in my script fails loudly.
24. As a person new to `tally`, I want the usage line to name `sentences`, `paragraphs` and `structure`, so that I can find them without reading the source.
25. As a maintainer, I want the new subcommands to print through the existing report formatter, so that every report has one shape.
26. As a maintainer, I want the new behaviour tested through the CLI's `run` function, so that the tests survive a change in how the counting is arranged inside.
27. As a maintainer, I want Sentence and Paragraph defined in the glossary, so that later work uses the same words for the same things.
28. As a maintainer, I want unknown commands to keep printing the usage line and exiting 2, so that adding subcommands breaks nothing that works today.

## Implementation Decisions

### Subcommands and reports

- The CLI gains three subcommands: `sentences`, `paragraphs` and `structure`. Each takes one file path.
- `sentences` and `paragraphs` each print a one-count report whose count is named after the subcommand.
- `structure` prints one report of two counts, in the fixed order sentences, paragraphs. It is a report of several counts, not a count of its own: no line named `structure` is ever printed.
- All three print through the existing report formatter, which is used as it is. Its interface and its `<name>: <number>` line format do not change.
- The CLI's command table today maps a subcommand to one count. It changes so that a subcommand names the ordered list of counts its report holds: one count for `sentences` and `paragraphs`, two for `structure`. The file is read once per run and every count in the report is taken from that one text.
- The `run` function keeps its contract: it takes the arguments and returns the exit code and the text to print, without touching the process. A printed report returns code 0. The returned text has no trailing line break.
- An unknown subcommand or a missing file still returns the usage line with code 2. The usage line names every subcommand the CLI accepts, so it now names `sentences`, `paragraphs` and `structure`.

### Counting

- Sentence counting and paragraph counting are two pure functions from the file's text to a number. They sit behind the CLI and are not part of its public surface.
- Whitespace has one meaning across `tally`: the one the glossary's Word already uses. "Holds a word" below means "holds at least one character that is not whitespace".

**Sentences**

- The ending marks are exactly the three characters `.`, `!` and `?`.
- Each unbroken run of ending marks ends one sentence, whatever comes before it. The sentence count is the number of such runs, plus one if the text after the last run holds a word. In a text with no ending mark at all, the whole text is that last run.
- Ending marks with anything between them, even one space, are separate runs: `What? !` has 2 sentences.
- Line breaks and blank lines do not end a sentence. Sentences and paragraphs are counted independently of each other.
- Abbreviations and numbers get no special treatment.

| Text | Sentences |
| --- | --- |
| (empty file) | 0 |
| ` \n\n` (only whitespace) | 0 |
| `Fine` | 1 |
| `Hello.` | 1 |
| `Hello.\n` | 1 |
| `What?!` | 1 |
| `Hello\nworld.` | 1 |
| `Title\n\nBody text.` | 1 |
| `Wait... what?` | 2 |
| `3.14` | 2 |
| `Hi! How are you?? Fine` | 3 |
| `e.g. this` | 3 |
| `...` | 1 |

**Paragraphs**

- The text is split into lines at `\n`. A line is blank when it holds no word, so an empty line and a line of only spaces or tabs are both blank.
- The paragraph count is the number of unbroken runs of lines that are not blank.
- A `\r` is whitespace, so a file with `\r\n` line endings gives the same count as the same text with `\n` endings, with no special handling.

| Text | Paragraphs |
| --- | --- |
| (empty file) | 0 |
| `\n\n\n` | 0 |
| ` \n\t\n` | 0 |
| `a` | 1 |
| `a\nb` | 1 |
| `\n\na\n\n` | 1 |
| `a\n\nb\n` | 2 |
| `a\nb\n\n\nc` | 2 |
| `a\n \t \nb` | 2 |
| `a\r\n\r\nb\r\n` | 2 |

**Structure**

| Text | Report |
| --- | --- |
| (empty file) | `sentences: 0` then `paragraphs: 0` |
| `Hi! How are you??\n\nFine` | `sentences: 3` then `paragraphs: 2` |

### Glossary

The glossary gains two terms, worded from the decisions:

- **Sentence**: a run of text ended by `.`, `!` or `?`, where several of them in a row end it once; a last run with no ending is a sentence if it holds a word.
- **Paragraph**: one or more lines in a row that are not blank; a line that holds only whitespace is blank.

## Testing Decisions

- A good test here checks only what a person running `tally` could see: the report text and the exit code. It does not import the counting functions, look inside the command table, or depend on how the counting is written.
- There is one seam, and it already exists: the CLI's `run` function, which returns the exit code and the output text without touching the process. Every new test calls it with a subcommand and a file path and compares the whole result. No new seam is added, and no child process is spawned.
- `run` reads a real file, so each test writes its text to a temporary file in the operating system's temporary directory and removes it afterwards. No way of passing text in directly is added for the tests' sake.
- The rows of the three tables above are the test cases: each row is one input text and one expected report, checked through `sentences`, `paragraphs` or `structure`. A table-driven loop over the rows is fine, as long as each row runs as its own named test.
- `structure` is also checked for agreement: for the same file, its two lines equal the lines printed by `sentences` and by `paragraphs`.
- Usage is checked for each new subcommand with the file left out: code 2, and the output names `sentences`, `paragraphs` and `structure`. The tests do not compare the whole usage line, because other subcommands are being added to it by separate work.
- The existing test for an unknown command keeps passing unchanged.
- The report formatter needs no new tests: it is not changed, and its line format is already covered.
- Prior art: the existing CLI test (an unknown command exits 2) and the existing formatter test (one line per count, in order). Both use Node's built-in test runner with strict assertions, one behaviour per test, and a test name that states the behaviour. The new tests follow that style and run under `npm test`.

## Out of Scope

- Reading from standard input.
- Several files in one run.
- Special treatment of abbreviations such as "e.g.", of decimal numbers, or of any other full stop that does not end a sentence in the reader's eyes. Each full stop ends a sentence.
- Ending marks other than `.`, `!` and `?`, such as `…` or the full stops of other scripts.
- The `words`, `lines`, `characters` and `all` subcommands, which belong to #1. `tally all` stays as #4 decided it (words, lines, characters) and does not gain sentences or paragraphs.
- What happens when the file does not exist or cannot be read. That behaviour is left as it is today.
- Flags, other output formats, and any change to the report's line format.

## Further Notes

- This spec is the result of the map in #5. The decisions it rests on are #6 (what a sentence is), #7 (what a paragraph is) and #8 (what `tally structure` prints).
- #1 adds `words`, `lines`, `characters` and `all` to the same command table and the same usage line. Neither piece of work depends on the other. Whichever lands second keeps the other's subcommands and merges the two. A command table in which a subcommand names a list of counts serves `all` as well as `structure`.
- Two points go one step past the wording of #6. Both follow from "each full stop ends a sentence", but neither has its own example in the decision, so the tables above pin them:
  - A run of ending marks with no text before it still ends a sentence, so a file holding only `...` has 1 sentence.
  - A blank line does not end a sentence, so a heading with no full stop runs into the sentence after it: `Title\n\nBody text.` has 1 sentence and 2 paragraphs.

nodes.title: Spec: word, line and character counts
nodes.body:
Spec for the wayfinder map #1. It turns that map's three decisions into one buildable feature: #2 (what a line is), #3 (what a character is) and #4 (what `tally all` prints).

## Problem Statement

`tally` exists to report counts about a text file, but it knows no counts yet. Whatever you type, it prints a usage message and exits with code 2. Someone who wants to know how many words, lines or characters a file holds gets nothing from it.

## Solution

`tally` learns three counts and four subcommands:

- `tally words <file>`, `tally lines <file>` and `tally characters <file>` each print a one-count report named after the subcommand.
- `tally all <file>` prints one report holding all three counts, always in the order words, lines, characters.

For a file containing `héllo 👋\nbye\n`:

```
$ tally words greeting.txt
words: 3

$ tally all greeting.txt
words: 3
lines: 2
characters: 12
```

What each count means:

- **words**: the number of words, as the glossary defines a word: a maximal run of non-whitespace characters.
- **lines**: a line is a run of characters ended by `\n`, plus a last run with no `\n` if it is non-empty. An empty file has 0 lines, and `\r\n` is one line ending.
- **characters**: a character is a Unicode code point, not a UTF-16 unit and not a byte. Line endings count like any other character.

## User Stories

1. As a tally user, I want `tally words <file>` to print the file's number of words, so that I can check a text against a word limit.
2. As a tally user, I want `tally lines <file>` to print the file's number of lines, so that I know how long a file is without opening it.
3. As a tally user, I want `tally characters <file>` to print the file's number of characters, so that I can check a text against a character limit.
4. As a tally user, I want `tally all <file>` to print the three counts in one report, so that one command gives me the whole picture.
5. As a tally user, I want the counts in `tally all` to always come in the order words, lines, characters, so that I can find each number in the same place every time.
6. As a tally user, I want each count printed on its own line as `<name>: <number>`, so that the report is easy to read.
7. As a tally user, I want a one-count report to be named after the subcommand I ran, so that the output says what was counted.
8. As a tally user, I want a count to have the same name and the same number whether I ask for it alone or through `tally all`, so that the two never disagree.
9. As a tally user, I want any run of spaces, tabs and line breaks between two words to separate them once, so that uneven spacing does not inflate the word count.
10. As a tally user, I want punctuation attached to a word to count as part of that word, so that `don't` and `stop.` are one word each.
11. As a tally user, I want a file holding only whitespace to report 0 words, so that blank files are not reported as having content.
12. As a tally user, I want a last line with no line ending to be counted, so that a file saved without a final newline is not short by one.
13. As a tally user, I want a final newline not to add an empty line to the count, so that `a\nb` and `a\nb\n` both report 2 lines.
14. As a tally user, I want blank lines to count as lines, so that the line count matches the line numbers my editor shows.
15. As a tally user on Windows, I want `\r\n` to count as one line ending, so that a file reports the same number of lines whichever system saved it.
16. As a tally user, I want an empty file to report 0 lines, so that nothing is not counted as one line.
17. As a tally user, I want an accented letter or an emoji stored as one code point to count as one character, so that `héllo 👋` reports 7 and the count does not depend on how the text is stored.
18. As a tally user, I want spaces and line endings to count as characters, so that the count covers everything in the file.
19. As a tally user, I want `tally all` on an empty file to print three zeros, so that an empty file is reported and not treated as an error.
20. As a tally user, I want a mistyped subcommand to print a usage line naming `words`, `lines`, `characters` and `all`, so that I can see what I should have typed.
21. As a tally user, I want the same usage line when I leave out the file, so that I learn the file is required.
22. As a script author, I want exit code 0 when a report is printed and exit code 2 when the arguments are wrong, so that my script can tell the two apart.
23. As a script author, I want the output to hold nothing but the report, so that I can parse it line by line.
24. As a script author, I want `tally all` to keep printing exactly these three counts when tally later learns others, so that my parsing does not break.
25. As a maintainer, I want each count defined once and used by both its own subcommand and `tally all`, so that the definitions cannot drift apart.
26. As a maintainer, I want every report to go through the existing report formatter, so that the output format lives in one place.
27. As a maintainer, I want the feature covered by tests that call the CLI the way a user would, so that I can change how counts are computed without rewriting tests.
28. As a contributor, I want line and character defined in the glossary next to word, so that later work uses the same meanings.

## Implementation Decisions

- **Modules.** A new counts module holds the three counts, each a pure function from a file's text to a number, with no I/O. The CLI module changes: its registry of counts gains the three entries, it learns the `all` subcommand, and its usage line names the new subcommands. The report formatter does not change.
- **One name per count.** A count's registry key is both its subcommand and its name in the report: `words`, `lines`, `characters`. The same function serves the single-count subcommand and `all`.
- **`all` is a subcommand, not a count.** It reads the file once, applies words, lines and characters to the same text, and passes the three name and number pairs to the report formatter in that order, in one call.
- **`all` is a fixed list.** It names exactly these three counts and does not loop over the registry. #4 decides "three counts", and #5 will add sentences and paragraphs to the same registry; `all` must still print three when that lands.
- **The `run` interface keeps its shape.** It takes the argument list and returns `{ code, out }` without touching the process. A known subcommand with a file gives code 0 and the report. An unknown subcommand or a missing file argument gives code 2 and the usage line, for `all` as for the other three.
- **Usage line.** `usage: tally <words|lines|characters|all> <file>`.
- **Words.** The number of maximal runs of non-whitespace characters. Whitespace is whatever JavaScript's regular-expression whitespace class matches: spaces, tabs, line endings and the other Unicode spaces.
- **Lines.** The number of `\n` in the text, plus one if the text is non-empty and does not end in `\n`. This is the definition from #2 written as arithmetic. Blank lines count. A `\r` is never a line ending by itself; `\r\n` counts once because it holds one `\n`.
- **Characters.** The number of code points in the decoded text, with no normalization and no grouping into what a reader sees as one symbol. `\r\n` is two characters, and a letter followed by a combining accent is two characters.
- **Reading.** The file is read once, as UTF-8, as it is today.
- **Glossary.** The project glossary gains **Line** and **Character**, worded as in #2 and #3, next to the existing **Word**.

Worked examples. The file contents are written with escapes; every number follows from the definitions above.

| File contents | words | lines | characters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (empty) | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `\n` | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| `a\nb` | 2 | 2 | 3 |
| `a\nb\n` | 2 | 2 | 4 |
| `a\r\nb\r\n` | 2 | 2 | 6 |
| `one  two\n\nthree` | 3 | 3 | 15 |
| `don't stop.` | 2 | 1 | 11 |
| `héllo 👋` | 2 | 1 | 7 |
| `héllo 👋\nbye\n` | 3 | 2 | 12 |

## Testing Decisions

- **What a good test is here.** It asserts what someone running the CLI sees: the exit code and the report text, for given arguments and file contents. It says nothing about how a count is computed or which module holds it.
- **One seam.** All new tests call the CLI module's `run` with an argument list and assert on the `{ code, out }` it returns. This is the seam the map names, and it already exists. No new seam is added, and the count functions are not tested directly.
- **File contents live in the test.** Each test writes the text it needs to a temporary file and passes that path to `run`, then removes it. Committed fixture files are avoided because an editor or git's line-ending handling can silently change a `\r\n` or a missing final newline, which are the cases under test.
- **Assert the whole output.** Compare `out` to the full expected string, such as `words: 3\nlines: 2\ncharacters: 12`, so that names, order and format are all covered.
- **Cases to cover.**
  - Each of `words`, `lines` and `characters` prints a one-count report named after the subcommand, with code 0.
  - `all` prints the three counts in the order words, lines, characters, with code 0.
  - An empty file reports 0 for every count.
  - Words: a mixed run of spaces, tabs and line breaks separates once; a whitespace-only file has 0 words.
  - Lines: the same count with and without a final newline; `\r\n` counts once; blank lines count.
  - Characters: `héllo 👋` is 7; line endings count; `\r\n` is two characters.
  - Usage: an unknown subcommand, and each of the four subcommands with no file, give code 2 and a usage line naming all four subcommands.
- **Prior art.** The existing CLI test calls `run` with an argument list and asserts on the result. The existing report formatter test asserts a whole multi-line report string. Both use Node's built-in test runner with strict assertions and run through `npm test`. The report formatter test stays as it is.

## Out of Scope

- Reading from standard input.
- Several files in one invocation.
- Bytes as a count.
- Sentences, paragraphs and `tally structure`, which belong to #5.
- A file that cannot be read. The map does not decide this, so the behaviour stays what it is today: `run` throws. Tests for this feature do not cover it.
- Encodings other than UTF-8, and any change to the report format.

## Further Notes

- **`all` will not mean "every count" for long.** Once #5 lands, tally will know five counts and `all` will print three of them. That follows from #4 as decided. If `all` should grow instead, that is a new decision to take before #5 is built, not something to change while building this.
- **A character is not always what a reader sees as one.** Code points are the decided unit (#3). An emoji with a skin tone, or a family emoji, is several code points and reports several characters. That is the definition working, not a bug to fix.
- **Both efforts touch the same two places.** This spec and #5 each add entries to the registry of counts and a group subcommand to the CLI module. Whichever is built second should expect to merge with the first.

All four tickets (#11, #12, #13, #15) are implemented and closed. The work is on the integration branch `spec-10-counts` (tip `cb65cfb`), not yet merged to `main`. This spec is left open until it is.

A two-axis code review (standards, spec) ran on the branch; its fixes are merged in `cb65cfb`: a count is now registered once and its subcommand follows from it, and the per-ticket usage tests were consolidated so each behaviour is asserted once. `npm test` passes with 34 tests.

## Parent

#9

## What to build

`tally sentences <file>` prints a one-count report, `sentences: <number>`, and exits 0. Today that command prints the usage line and exits 2.

A **sentence** is a run of text ended by `.`, `!` or `?`. Several of them in a row end it once. A last run with no ending is also a sentence if it holds a word.

As a rule for counting: the sentence count is the number of unbroken runs of ending marks, plus one if the text after the last run holds a word. "Holds a word" means "holds at least one character that is not whitespace", the same whitespace the glossary's Word uses. In a text with no ending mark at all, the whole text is that last run.

- The ending marks are exactly `.`, `!` and `?`.
- Ending marks with anything between them, even one space, are separate runs.
- Line breaks and blank lines do not end a sentence.
- Abbreviations and numbers get no special treatment: each full stop ends a sentence.

| Text | Sentences |
| --- | --- |
| (empty file) | 0 |
| ` \n\n` (only whitespace) | 0 |
| `Fine` | 1 |
| `Hello.` | 1 |
| `Hello.\n` | 1 |
| `What?!` | 1 |
| `Hello\nworld.` | 1 |
| `Title\n\nBody text.` | 1 |
| `...` | 1 |
| `What? !` | 2 |
| `Wait... what?` | 2 |
| `3.14` | 2 |
| `Hi! How are you?? Fine` | 3 |
| `e.g. this` | 3 |

The count prints through the existing report formatter, which does not change. The counting is a pure function from the file's text to a number. It sits behind the CLI, and the tests reach it only through the CLI's `run` function.

This is the first slice of #9, so it also settles how the CLI tests hand a file to `run`: each test writes its text to a temporary file in the operating system's temporary directory and removes it afterwards. The paragraph and structure tickets reuse that arrangement, so build it to be reused.

- [ ] Every row of the table above gives the listed number, and each row runs as its own named test.

- [ ] The existing test for an unknown command passes unchanged.
- [ ] The new tests call only `run`, with the path of a temporary file, and compare the returned code and text. They do not import the counting function and do not spawn a process.
- [ ] The glossary gains **Sentence**: a run of text ended by `.`, `!` or `?`, where several of them in a row end it once; a last run with no ending is a sentence if it holds a word.
- [ ] `npm test` passes.

## Parent

#9

## What to build

`tally structure <file>` prints one report holding two counts, sentences first and paragraphs second, and exits 0. Today that command prints the usage line and exits 2.

For a file holding `Hi! How are you??`, a blank line, then `Fine`:

```
$ tally structure notes.txt
sentences: 3
paragraphs: 2
```

`structure` is a report of several counts, not a count of its own: no line named `structure` is ever printed. The two counts are the ones `tally sentences` (#14) and `tally paragraphs` (#16) already print, so the numbers always agree with those two subcommands. The file is read once per run, and both counts are taken from that one text.

Work in two steps:

1. Make the change easy. The CLI's command table maps a subcommand to one count. Reshape it so a subcommand names the ordered list of counts its report holds, with a list of one for each subcommand that exists. Nothing a user can see changes in this step, and every test stays green.

| Text | Report |
| --- | --- |
| (empty file) | `sentences: 0` then `paragraphs: 0` |

#10 adds `all`, which is also a report of several counts, to the same command table. If it is there when you start, the reshaped table serves it too. `all` stays as words, lines, characters and does not gain sentences or paragraphs.

- [ ] `tally structure <file>` returns code 0 and a two-line report, `sentences: <number>` then `paragraphs: <number>`, with no trailing line break, printed through the existing report formatter.

nodes.title: Spec: digit and punctuation counts (`digits`, `punctuation`, `symbols`)
nodes.body:
Spec for the wayfinder map #22. It turns that map's three decisions into one buildable feature: #23 (what a digit is), #24 (what a punctuation mark is) and #25 (what `tally symbols` prints).

## Problem Statement

`tally` reports counts about a text file, but it cannot say how many digits or punctuation marks a file holds. Someone who wants to know how number-heavy a text is, or how heavily it is punctuated, has no subcommand to ask: `tally digits notes.txt` and `tally punctuation notes.txt` both print the usage line and exit 2. There is also no way to get both numbers in one report.

## Solution

Three new subcommands, each taking one file:

- `tally digits <file>` prints a one-count report: `digits: <number>`.
- `tally punctuation <file>` prints a one-count report: `punctuation: <number>`.
- `tally symbols <file>` prints one report holding both counts, digits first.

For a file holding `Call 555-0199, now!`:

```
$ tally digits note.txt
digits: 7
$ tally punctuation note.txt
punctuation: 3
$ tally symbols note.txt
digits: 7
punctuation: 3
```

A **digit** is one of the ten ASCII characters `0` to `9`. No other Unicode digit counts.

A **punctuation mark** is one of the 32 ASCII punctuation characters: ``!"#$%&'()*+,-./:;<=>?@[\]^_`{|}~``. Nothing outside ASCII counts.

Every digit and every punctuation mark in the file counts once, wherever it stands. An empty file has 0 digits and 0 punctuation marks.

## User Stories

1. As a tally user, I want `tally digits <file>` to print how many digits my file holds, so that I can see how number-heavy a text is.
2. As a tally user, I want `tally punctuation <file>` to print how many punctuation marks my file holds, so that I can see how heavily a text is punctuated.
3. As a tally user, I want `tally symbols <file>` to print both counts in one report, so that I do not have to run `tally` twice.
4. As a tally user, I want each of the ten characters `0` to `9` to count as a digit, so that the count matches the digits I can type on any keyboard.
5. As a tally user, I want every digit of a number to count, so that `2026` reports 4 digits and not 1 number.
6. As a tally user, I want digits inside a word to count, so that `a1b22` reports 3.
7. As a tally user, I want digits of other scripts, such as `٣` or the full-width `１`, not to count, so that one fixed rule explains every count.
8. As a tally user, I want each of the 32 ASCII punctuation characters to count as a punctuation mark, so that the count covers every mark on a plain keyboard.
9. As a tally user, I want characters such as `$`, `+`, `=`, `_` and `~` to count as punctuation marks, so that I do not have to guess which keyboard marks are "real" punctuation.
10. As a tally user, I want every mark in a row of marks to count, so that `...` reports 3 and `?!` reports 2.
11. As a tally user, I want a mark attached to a word to count, so that `don't stop.` reports 2.
12. As a tally user, I want typographic marks outside ASCII, such as `«`, `»`, curly quotes, `…` and `—`, not to count, so that the same fixed rule explains every count.
13. As a tally user, I want letters, spaces, tabs and line endings to count as neither a digit nor a punctuation mark, so that the two counts measure only what their names say.
14. As a tally user, I want a character never to count as both a digit and a punctuation mark, so that the two numbers in `tally symbols` never overlap.
15. As a tally user, I want a mark between digits to count as punctuation and the digits around it as digits, so that `3.14` reports 3 digits and 1 punctuation mark.
16. As a tally user, I want an empty file to report `digits: 0`, so that an empty file is reported and not treated as an error.
17. As a tally user, I want an empty file to report `punctuation: 0`, for the same reason.
18. As a tally user, I want a file of only whitespace to report 0 for both counts, so that blank files are not reported as having content.
19. As a tally user, I want a file with `\r\n` line endings to give the same two counts as the same text with `\n` endings, so that the counts do not depend on my editor.
20. As a tally user, I want the symbols report to list digits first and punctuation second every time, so that I always know where to look.
21. As a tally user, I want `tally symbols` on an empty file to print two zeros, so that the report always has the same two lines.
22. As a script author, I want every count printed on its own line as `<name>: <number>`, so that I can parse these reports the same way as any other `tally` report.
23. As a script author, I want a one-count report to carry the name of the subcommand I ran, so that the output names match what I typed.
24. As a script author, I want `tally symbols` to print the same names and the same numbers that `tally digits` and `tally punctuation` print for the same file, so that I can use either form.
25. As a script author, I want `tally symbols` to keep printing exactly these two counts when `tally` later learns others, so that my parsing does not break.
26. As a script author, I want the output to hold nothing but the report, so that I can parse it line by line.
27. As a script author, I want exit code 0 whenever a report is printed, so that I can detect success.
28. As a script author, I want each new subcommand to print the usage line and exit 2 when I leave out the file, so that a mistake in my script fails loudly.
29. As a person new to `tally`, I want the usage line to name `digits`, `punctuation` and `symbols`, so that I can find them without reading the source.
30. As a maintainer, I want each count defined once and used by both its own subcommand and `tally symbols`, so that the two cannot drift apart.
31. As a maintainer, I want the new subcommands to print through the existing report formatter, so that every report has one shape.
32. As a maintainer, I want the new behaviour tested through the CLI's `run` function, so that the tests survive a change in how the counting is arranged inside.
33. As a maintainer, I want unknown commands to keep printing the usage line and exiting 2, so that adding subcommands breaks nothing that works today.
34. As a contributor, I want Digit and Punctuation mark defined in the glossary, so that later work uses the same words for the same things.

## Implementation Decisions

### Subcommands and reports

- The CLI gains three subcommands: `digits`, `punctuation` and `symbols`. Each takes one file path.
- `digits` and `punctuation` each print a one-count report whose count is named after the subcommand.
- `symbols` prints one report of two counts, in the fixed order digits, punctuation. It is a report of several counts, not a count of its own: no line named `symbols` is ever printed.
- `symbols` is a fixed list of exactly these two counts. It does not grow when `tally` learns other counts.
- One name per count. A count has the same name, `digits` or `punctuation`, and the same number whether it is asked for alone or through `symbols`. The same counting serves both.
- All three print through the existing report formatter, which is used as it is. Its interface and its `<name>: <number>` line format do not change.
- The CLI's command table on `main` maps a subcommand to one count. It changes so that a subcommand names the ordered list of counts its report holds: one count for `digits` and for `punctuation`, two for `symbols`. The file is read once per run, as UTF-8 as it is today, and every count in the report is taken from that one text.
- The `run` function keeps its contract: it takes the arguments and returns the exit code and the text to print, without touching the process. A printed report returns code 0. The returned text has no trailing line break.
- An unknown subcommand or a missing file still returns the usage line with code 2, for `symbols` as for the other two. The usage line names every subcommand the CLI accepts, so it now names `digits`, `punctuation` and `symbols`. With nothing else built, it reads `usage: tally <digits|punctuation|symbols> <file>`.

### Counting

- Digit counting and punctuation counting are two pure functions from the file's text to a number, with no I/O. They sit behind the CLI and are not part of its public surface. Where they live follows the arrangement of counts found on `main` when this is built. If there is none yet, one module for the two is enough.
- Both counts go character by character through the decoded text. Each character is judged by itself: its neighbours, the word it is in and the line it is on play no part. Nothing is grouped and no run is collapsed.
- The two sets share no character, so no character adds to both counts. Letters, whitespace, control characters and every character outside ASCII add to neither.

**Digits**

- The digits are exactly the ten characters `0` to `9` (U+0030 to U+0039).
- This is not Unicode's digit class. Digits of other scripts and full-width digits are not digits.

**Punctuation marks**

- The punctuation marks are exactly these 32 characters: ``!"#$%&'()*+,-./:;<=>?@[\]^_`{|}~``. They are every printable ASCII character that is not a letter, a digit or the space: U+0021 to U+002F, U+003A to U+0040, U+005B to U+0060 and U+007B to U+007E.
- This is not Unicode's punctuation category. That category leaves out nine of the 32 (`$`, `+`, `<`, `=`, `>`, `^`, `` ` ``, `|` and `~`, which Unicode files under symbols) and takes in marks outside ASCII. The set is the list above, written out or given as those four ranges.
- Every occurrence counts: `...` holds 3 punctuation marks.

**Worked examples.** Texts are written with escapes. Every number follows from the definitions above.

| Text | digits | punctuation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (empty file) | 0 | 0 |
| ` \n\t\n` (only whitespace) | 0 | 0 |
| `a1b22` | 3 | 0 |
| `0123456789` | 10 | 0 |
| `٣` (Arabic-Indic three, U+0663) | 0 | 0 |
| `１２３` (full-width digits, U+FF11 to U+FF13) | 0 | 0 |
| `Hi, you!` | 0 | 2 |
| `don't stop.` | 0 | 2 |
| `snake_case` | 0 | 1 |
| `Wait... what?!` | 0 | 5 |
| `«hi»` | 0 | 0 |
| `“Wait…” — no` (curly quotes, ellipsis character, em dash) | 0 | 0 |
| (the 32 punctuation marks, each once) | 0 | 32 |
| `3.14` | 3 | 1 |
| `2026-11-16` | 8 | 2 |
| `$5 + 5% = ?` | 2 | 5 |
| `Call 555-0199, now!` | 7 | 3 |
| `1\r\n2\r\n` | 2 | 0 |
| (every printable ASCII character, space to `~`, each once) | 10 | 32 |
| `1️⃣` (keycap one: U+0031, U+FE0F, U+20E3) | 1 | 0 |

**Symbols**

| Text | Report |
| --- | --- |
| (empty file) | `digits: 0` then `punctuation: 0` |
| `Call 555-0199, now!` | `digits: 7` then `punctuation: 3` |

### Glossary

The glossary gains two terms, worded from the decisions:

- **Digit**: one of the ten ASCII characters `0` to `9`. No other Unicode digit is a digit.
- **Punctuation mark**: one of the 32 ASCII punctuation characters, ``!"#$%&'()*+,-./:;<=>?@[\]^_`{|}~``. Nothing outside ASCII is a punctuation mark.

"Symbol" does not become a glossary term. `symbols` is only the name of the subcommand that prints the two counts.

## Testing Decisions

- A good test here checks only what a person running `tally` could see: the report text and the exit code, for given arguments and file contents. It does not import the counting functions, look inside the command table, or depend on how the counting is written.
- There is one seam, and it already exists: the CLI's `run` function, which returns the exit code and the output text without touching the process. This is the seam the map names. Every new test calls it with a subcommand and a file path and compares the whole result. No new seam is added, and no child process is spawned.
- `run` reads a real file, so each test writes its text to a temporary file in the operating system's temporary directory and removes it afterwards. The text stays in the test, next to the number it should give. No committed fixture files are added, and no way of passing text in directly is added for the tests' sake.
- Assert the whole output. Compare the result to the full expected report, such as `digits: 7` then `punctuation: 3`, so that names, order and format are all covered.
- The rows of the two tables above are the test cases: each row is one input text and one expected report, checked through `digits`, `punctuation` or `symbols`. A table-driven loop over the rows is fine, as long as each row runs as its own named test.
- The rows that hold characters outside ASCII are the ones that prove the ASCII-only rule. In the test source, write those characters so that a reader can tell which character is meant, by escape or by a name in the test's title.
- Two rows guard the punctuation set as a whole and must not be dropped: the 32 marks each once (32), and every printable ASCII character each once (10 digits, 32 punctuation marks). Together they fail if a mark is missing, if a letter or the space is counted, or if a Unicode category was used in place of the list.
- `symbols` is also checked for agreement: for the same file, its two lines equal the lines printed by `digits` and by `punctuation`.
- Usage is checked for each new subcommand with the file left out: code 2, and the output names `digits`, `punctuation` and `symbols`. The tests do not compare the whole usage line, because other subcommands are being added to it by separate work.
- The existing test for an unknown command keeps passing unchanged.
- The report formatter needs no new tests: it is not changed, and its line format is already covered.
- Prior art: the existing CLI test (an unknown command exits 2) and the existing formatter test (one line per count, in order, compared as one whole string). Both use Node's built-in test runner with strict assertions, one behaviour per test, and a test name that states the behaviour. The new tests follow that style and run under `npm test`.

## Out of Scope

- Unicode digits and punctuation outside ASCII. They count as neither, and that is the rule, not a gap.
- Reading from standard input.
- Several files in one run.
- Counting numbers. `2026` is 4 digits, not 1 number.
- Counts of letters, of whitespace, or of characters that are neither a digit nor a punctuation mark.
- The subcommands of the other efforts: `words`, `lines`, `characters` and `all` (#1), `sentences`, `paragraphs` and `structure` (#5), and `longest-word`, `longest-line` and `longest` (#18). `all` and `structure` stay as decided and do not gain digits or punctuation.
- What happens when the file does not exist or cannot be read. That behaviour is left as it is today.
- Encodings other than UTF-8.
- Flags, other output formats, and any change to the report's line format.

## Further Notes

- **Where `main` stands.** When this spec was written, `main` knew no counts: every command printed the usage line. The specs #10 (for #1) and #9 (for #5) were built on the integration branches `spec-10-counts` and `spec-9-sentence-paragraph-counts`, neither merged yet, and #18 had no spec. This spec is written against `main` and depends on none of them.
- **Four efforts touch the same places.** Each adds subcommands to the command table and the usage line, terms to the glossary, and tests to the CLI's test file. Whichever lands later keeps the others' subcommands and merges. Both integration branches already turned the command table into one where a subcommand names a list of counts, which is the shape this spec asks for. If one of them is on `main` by then, add to its table and do not reshape it.
- **Points that go one step past the wording of the decisions.** Each follows from them, but none has its own example there, so the tables above pin them:
  - "ASCII punctuation" is the list of 32, not Unicode's punctuation category. #24 writes the list out, and nine of its characters are symbols in Unicode's eyes.
  - Each mark counts by itself, so `...` holds 3 punctuation marks. This differs on purpose from Sentence in #6, where a run of ending marks ends a sentence once. The two do not affect each other.
  - A mark between digits is a punctuation mark and the digits around it are digits: `3.14` has 3 digits and 1 punctuation mark.
  - Nothing is grouped into what a reader sees as one symbol. A keycap emoji such as `1️⃣` is stored as the ASCII character `1` followed by two other code points, so it holds 1 digit. That is the definition working, not a bug to fix. #3 takes the same line for characters.
- **"Subcommand" is not in the glossary**, although the maps, the specs and the code all use it. This spec scopes the glossary change to Digit and Punctuation mark. The gap is one for a domain-modeling pass, as already noted on #10.

nodes.title: Spec: longest word and longest line (`longest-word`, `longest-line`, `longest`)
nodes.body:
Spec for the wayfinder map #18. It turns that map's three decisions into one buildable feature: #19 (what `tally longest-word` reports), #20 (what `tally longest-line` reports) and #21 (what `tally longest` prints).

## Problem Statement

`tally` reports counts about a text file, but it cannot say how long the file's longest word or longest line is. Someone checking a file against a line-length limit, or wondering whether one long word will overflow a narrow column, has no subcommand to ask: `tally longest-word notes.txt` and `tally longest-line notes.txt` both print the usage line and exit 2. There is also no way to get both numbers in one report.

## Solution

Three new subcommands, each taking one file:

- `tally longest-word <file>` prints a one-count report: `longest-word: <number>`.
- `tally longest-line <file>` prints a one-count report: `longest-line: <number>`.
- `tally longest <file>` prints one report holding both counts, longest-word first.

For a file containing `a héllo 👋👋\nbye\n`:

```
$ tally longest-word greeting.txt
longest-word: 5

$ tally longest-line greeting.txt
longest-line: 10

$ tally longest greeting.txt
longest-word: 5
longest-line: 10
```

What each count means:

- **longest-word**: the length of the file's longest word, where a word is what the glossary says it is: a maximal run of non-whitespace characters. A file with no word reports 0.
- **longest-line**: the length of the file's longest line. The line ending is not part of the line and is not counted. `\n` and `\r\n` both end a line. An empty file reports 0.

Both lengths are in Unicode code points, not UTF-16 units and not bytes.

## User Stories

1. As a tally user, I want `tally longest-word <file>` to print the length of the file's longest word, so that I can tell whether any word will overflow a narrow column.
2. As a tally user, I want `tally longest-line <file>` to print the length of the file's longest line, so that I can check a file against a line-length limit without opening it.
3. As a tally user, I want `tally longest <file>` to print both counts in one report, so that I do not have to run `tally` twice.
4. As a tally user, I want the counts in `tally longest` to always come in the order longest-word, longest-line, so that I find each number in the same place every time.
5. As a tally user, I want each count printed on its own line as `<name>: <number>`, so that these reports read like every other `tally` report.
6. As a tally user, I want a one-count report to be named after the subcommand I ran, so that the output says what was measured.
7. As a tally user, I want a count to have the same name and the same number whether I ask for it alone or through `tally longest`, so that the two never disagree.
8. As a tally user, I want `tally longest` to print only its two counts and no line named `longest`, so that every line of the report is a real count.
9. As a tally user, I want a word's length measured in code points, so that `héllo` is 5 and `👋👋` is 2 however the text is stored.
10. As a tally user, I want punctuation attached to a word to count toward its length, so that `stop.` is 5 and I can explain the number by looking at the text.
11. As a tally user, I want any whitespace (a space, a tab, a line ending) to end a word, so that a word never runs across two lines.
12. As a tally user, I want a file with no word, whether empty or holding only whitespace, to report `longest-word: 0`, so that a blank file gives an answer and not an error.
13. As a tally user, I want several words tied for longest to report that one length, so that a tie changes nothing.
14. As a tally user, I want the line ending left out of a line's length, so that the number matches the column my editor shows at the end of the line.
15. As a tally user on Windows, I want `\r\n` treated as one line ending with neither character counted, so that the same text reports the same length whichever system saved it.
16. As a tally user, I want a last line with no line ending measured like any other line, so that a file saved without a final newline is not under-reported.
17. As a tally user, I want a final line ending not to change the result, so that `ab\nabcd` and `ab\nabcd\n` both report 4.
18. As a tally user, I want spaces inside a line, trailing spaces included, to count toward its length, so that whitespace pushing a line over a limit is not hidden.
19. As a tally user, I want a tab to count as one, so that the number does not depend on anyone's tab-width setting.
20. As a tally user, I want a line's length measured in code points, so that an emoji or an accented letter stored as one code point adds one.
21. As a tally user, I want an empty file to report `longest-line: 0`, so that nothing is not reported as something.
22. As a tally user, I want a file holding only blank lines to report `longest-line: 0`, so that empty lines have no length.
23. As a tally user, I want a line holding only whitespace to still have its length while holding no word, so that the two counts each answer their own question.
24. As a tally user, I want `tally longest` on an empty file to print two zeros, so that an empty file is reported and not treated as an error.
25. As a tally user, I want a mistyped subcommand to print a usage line naming `longest-word`, `longest-line` and `longest`, so that I can see what I should have typed.
26. As a tally user, I want the same usage line when I leave out the file, so that I learn the file is required.
27. As a script author, I want exit code 0 when a report is printed and exit code 2 when the arguments are wrong, so that my script can tell the two apart.
28. As a script author, I want the output to hold nothing but the report, so that I can parse it line by line.
29. As a script author, I want subcommands matched exactly, so that a typo such as `longest-words` fails loudly and never runs `longest`.
30. As a script author, I want `tally longest` to keep printing exactly these two counts when `tally` later learns others, so that my parsing does not break.
31. As a maintainer, I want each count defined once and used by both its own subcommand and `longest`, so that the definitions cannot drift apart.
32. As a maintainer, I want every report to go through the existing report formatter, so that the output format lives in one place.
33. As a maintainer, I want `longest-word` to find words the way the glossary defines them, so that it can never disagree with a word count about what a word is.
34. As a maintainer, I want length in code points worked out in one place for both counts, so that a word and a line are never measured in different units.
35. As a maintainer, I want the feature covered by tests that call the CLI the way a user would, so that I can change how the counts are computed without rewriting tests.
36. As a maintainer, I want unknown commands to keep printing the usage line and exiting 2, including names every JavaScript object carries such as `toString`, so that adding subcommands breaks nothing and hides no surprise.
37. As a contributor, I want this feature to build on `main` as it stands, without waiting for the other counts, so that it can be picked up now.

## Implementation Decisions

### Subcommands and reports

- The CLI gains three subcommands: `longest-word`, `longest-line` and `longest`. Each takes one file path.
- `longest-word` and `longest-line` each print a one-count report whose count is named after the subcommand.
- `longest` prints one report of two counts, in the fixed order longest-word, longest-line. It is a subcommand, not a count: no line named `longest` is ever printed.
- **One name per count.** A count's name is both its subcommand and its name in a report. The same function serves the single-count subcommand and `longest`.
- **`longest` is a fixed list.** It names exactly these two counts and does not grow when `tally` learns others.
- **The command table changes shape.** Today it maps a subcommand to one count and names the report's only line after the subcommand. It changes so that a subcommand names the ordered list of counts its report holds: one count for `longest-word` and for `longest-line`, two for `longest`. The file is read once per run and every count in the report is taken from that one text.
- **Subcommands are matched exactly.** `longest`, `longest-word` and `longest-line` are three separate entries. There is no prefix matching, so `longest-` and `longest-words` are unknown.
- **Looking a subcommand up finds only the subcommands `tally` defines.** A name that every JavaScript object carries, such as `toString` or `constructor`, is an unknown subcommand like any other. On `main` today `tally toString <file>` prints `toString: [object Undefined]` with code 0; after this work it prints the usage line with code 2.
- All three subcommands print through the existing report formatter, used as it is. Its interface and its `<name>: <number>` line format do not change.
- **The `run` interface keeps its shape.** It takes the argument list and returns `{ code, out }` without touching the process. A known subcommand with a file gives code 0 and the report. An unknown subcommand or a missing file gives code 2 and the usage line, for `longest` as for the other two. The returned text has no trailing line break.
- **Usage line.** It names every subcommand the CLI accepts, so it now names `longest-word`, `longest-line` and `longest`. On `main` as it stands, where `tally` knows no other subcommand, it reads `usage: tally <longest-word|longest-line|longest> <file>`. The placeholder it shows while `tally` knows no count can no longer be reached and goes.

### Counting

- **Modules.** A counts module holds the two counts, each a pure function from a file's text to a number, with no I/O. `main` has no such module today, so this work creates it; if one exists by the time this is built, the two counts join it. The counts sit behind the CLI module and are not part of its public surface.
- **Length.** The length of a word or a line is its number of code points in the decoded text, with no normalization and no grouping into what a reader sees as one symbol. Both counts measure with the same piece of code.
- **Reading.** The file is read once, as UTF-8, as it is today.

**Longest word**

- Words are found as the glossary defines them: maximal runs of non-whitespace characters. Whitespace is whatever JavaScript's regular-expression whitespace class matches: spaces, tabs, `\r`, `\n` and the other Unicode spaces. This is the meaning #10 gives whitespace, so `tally` has one.
- The count is the largest length among the file's words, and 0 when the file has no word.
- Punctuation attached to a word is part of it. A word never spans a line ending.

**Longest line**

- A line ending is `\r\n`, or a `\n` with no `\r` before it. The text is cut at every line ending, and the count is the largest length among the pieces. An empty text gives 0.
- A `\r` with no `\n` after it is not a line ending. It stays in its line and counts as one code point, in the middle of a line or at the very end of the file.
- Whitespace inside a line counts, leading and trailing included. A tab counts as one.
- A last line with no line ending is measured like any other. A final line ending adds nothing.
- These are the same lines #2 defines for the line count (a run of characters ended by `\n`, plus a non-empty last run; `\r\n` is one line ending). This count measures them and adds no second meaning of line.

**Worked examples.** File contents are written with escapes. Every number follows from the definitions above and was checked by running them.

| File contents | longest-word | longest-line | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (empty) | 0 | 0 | An empty file reports 0 for both |
| `\n\n\n` | 0 | 0 | Blank lines have no length |
| `\t \t\n` | 0 | 3 | Whitespace is no word, but it has length in a line |
| `a` | 1 | 1 | |
| `a héllo 👋👋` | 5 | 10 | The example in #19 |
| `a héllo 👋👋\nbye\n` | 5 | 10 | The example in the Solution |
| `ab\r\nabcd\n` | 4 | 4 | The example in #20: `\r\n` is not counted |
| `ab\nabcd` | 4 | 4 | A last line with no line ending is measured |
| `abcd\nab\n` | 4 | 4 | The longest need not come last; a final line ending adds nothing |
| `one  two\n\nthree` | 5 | 8 | Two spaces inside a line both count |
| `don't stop.` | 5 | 11 | Punctuation is part of a word |
| `ab   \nabc` | 3 | 5 | Three trailing spaces count toward the line |
| `x\ty` | 1 | 3 | A tab ends a word and counts as one in a line |
| `ab\ncdef gh` | 4 | 7 | The longest word and the longest line are found independently |
| `👋👋👋 ab` | 3 | 6 | Code points, not UTF-16 units (which would give 6 and 9) |
| `a\rb` | 1 | 3 | A lone `\r` is whitespace, so it ends a word, but it is not a line ending |
| `ab\r` | 2 | 3 | A `\r` at the end of the file with no `\n` is counted |
| `é` | 2 | 2 | `e` followed by a combining acute accent is two code points |

### Glossary

No change. Longest word and longest line are counts built on **Word**, which the glossary has, and on Line, which #2 decided and #10 adds to the glossary together with Character. This work does not write a second definition of either.

## Testing Decisions

- **What a good test is here.** It asserts what someone running the CLI sees: the exit code and the report text, for given arguments and file contents. It does not import the count functions, look inside the command table, or depend on how a length is computed.
- **One seam.** Every new test calls the CLI module's `run` with an argument list and asserts on the `{ code, out }` it returns. This is the seam the map names, and it already exists. No new seam is added, the counts module is not tested directly, and no child process is spawned.
- **File contents live in the test.** `run` reads a real file, so each test writes its text to a temporary file in the operating system's temporary directory and removes it when the test ends. Committed fixture files are avoided because an editor or git's line-ending handling can silently change a `\r\n` or a missing final newline, which are the cases under test. No way of passing text in directly is added for the tests' sake.
- **Assert the whole result.** Compare the result to the full expected value, such as `{ code: 0, out: 'longest-word: 5' }`, and for `longest` the full two-line text, so that names, order and format are all covered.
- **The rows of the table are the test cases.** Each row is checked through `longest-word` and through `longest-line`. A table-driven loop is fine as long as each row runs as its own named test.
- **`longest`.** It prints both counts in the order longest-word, longest-line with code 0, checked at least on the empty file (two zeros) and on the Solution's example. It is also checked for agreement: for the same file, its two lines equal the lines `longest-word` and `longest-line` print.
- **Usage.** Each of the three subcommands with the file left out gives code 2 and a usage line naming all three. The names are checked as whole alternatives of the usage line, not as substrings: `longest` is contained in `longest-word`, so a substring check would pass with `longest` missing. The tests do not compare the whole usage line, because other work adds subcommands to it.
- **Unknown subcommands.** `longest-words` and `longest-`, given a real file, give code 2 and the usage line. So do `toString`, `constructor` and `__proto__`.
- **What stays as it is.** The existing test for an unknown command keeps passing unchanged. The report formatter is not changed and gets no new tests.
- **Prior art.** On `main`: the existing CLI test, which calls `run` with an argument list, and the existing formatter test, which asserts a whole multi-line report. Both use Node's built-in test runner with strict assertions, one behaviour per test, a test name that states the behaviour, and run through `npm test`. The integration branches for #10 and #9 hold fuller examples of the same approach: a small helper that writes a text to a temporary file tied to the test's lifetime, whole-result assertions and, in #9's case, table-driven rows. Neither branch is on `main`, so this work writes its own helper in the same style.

## Out of Scope

- Printing the longest word or the longest line itself, or saying where it is in the file.
- Reading from standard input.
- Several files in one invocation.
- Display width. A tab is one code point whatever its tab stop, and a wide character is one. A symbol a reader sees as one but that is stored as several code points counts as several.
- Normalization, and any special treatment of a byte order mark. A byte order mark is a code point like any other: it adds one to the first line's length, and being whitespace it never lengthens a word.
- Line endings other than `\n` and `\r\n`: a lone `\r` and the Unicode line separators do not end a line.
- The other counts and their subcommands: `words`, `lines`, `characters` and `all` (#10), `sentences`, `paragraphs` and `structure` (#9), and `digits`, `punctuation` and `symbols` (#26). `all`, `structure` and `symbols` do not gain the two new counts.
- A file that cannot be read. The map does not decide this, so the behaviour stays what it is today: `run` throws. Tests for this feature do not cover it.
- Flags, other output formats, encodings other than UTF-8, and any change to the report's line format.

## Further Notes

- **Where this goes one step past the decisions.** Each point below follows from the wording of #19 to #21 but has no example of its own there, so the table pins it. If any of them is not what was meant, that is a decision to revisit before building, not during.
  - A `\r` with no `\n` after it is counted as part of its line (`a\rb` is 3, `ab\r` is 3). #20 names `\n` and `\r\n` as the line endings, so nothing else is one.
  - A line of only whitespace has a length while holding no word (`\t \t\n` reports 0 and 3).
  - Whitespace means JavaScript's regular-expression whitespace class. The glossary says "non-whitespace" without listing it; #10 settled on this class and this spec follows it.
- **One decision comes from the code, not the map.** That a name such as `toString` is an unknown subcommand is not in #18. The reviews of #10 and #9 each found and fixed this on their branches, and `main` still has it. It is included here so that this work does not ship the same fault a third time. It can be dropped from this spec without touching anything else.
- **Length is not always what a reader sees.** Code points are the decided unit. An emoji with a skin tone or a family emoji is several code points, and so is a letter with a combining accent. That is the definition working, not a bug to fix.
- **`main` knows no counts yet.** The work for #10 and #9 is finished but sits on the integration branches `spec-10-counts` and `spec-9-sentence-paragraph-counts`, neither merged to `main`, and #26 (digits and punctuation, from map #22) is specified but not built. This feature depends on none of them and builds from `main`. All four add entries to the same command table and the same usage line, and all of them use the shape decided here, a subcommand naming an ordered list of counts. Whichever lands later keeps the others' subcommands and merges the tables, the test helpers and, where there are two, the counts modules.
- **"Subcommand" is not in the glossary.** The map, the earlier specs and this one all use the word. Adding it is glossary work for `/domain-modeling`, not for this build.

## Parent

#26

## What to build

`tally digits <file>` prints a one-count report, `digits: <number>`, and exits 0. Today that command prints the usage line and exits 2.

A **digit** is one of the ten ASCII characters `0` to `9`. No other Unicode digit counts.

As a rule for counting: go character by character through the file's text and count each character that is one of `0` to `9` (U+0030 to U+0039). Each character is judged by itself: its neighbours, the word it is in and the line it is on play no part.

- Every digit of a number counts: `2026` holds 4 digits, not 1 number.
- This is not Unicode's digit class. Digits of other scripts and full-width digits are not digits.
- Letters, whitespace, punctuation marks and every character outside ASCII add nothing.
- Nothing is grouped into what a reader sees as one symbol. A keycap emoji is stored as an ASCII digit followed by two other code points, so it holds 1 digit.

Texts are written with escapes.

| Text | Digits |
| --- | --- |
| (empty file) | 0 |
| ` \n\t\n` (only whitespace) | 0 |
| `Hi, you!` | 0 |
| `٣` (Arabic-Indic three, U+0663) | 0 |
| `１２３` (full-width digits, U+FF11 to U+FF13) | 0 |
| `1️⃣` (keycap one: U+0031, U+FE0F, U+20E3) | 1 |
| `$5 + 5% = ?` | 2 |
| `1\r\n2\r\n` | 2 |
| `a1b22` | 3 |
| `3.14` | 3 |
| `Call 555-0199, now!` | 7 |
| `2026-11-16` | 8 |
| `0123456789` | 10 |
| (every printable ASCII character, space to `~`, each once) | 10 |

The count prints through the existing report formatter, which does not change. The counting is a pure function from the file's text to a number, with no I/O. It sits behind the CLI, and the tests reach it only through the CLI's `run` function. The file is read once per run, as UTF-8 as it is today.

`run` reads a real file, so each test writes its text to a temporary file in the operating system's temporary directory and removes it afterwards. The text stays in the test, next to the number it should give. In the test source, write the characters outside ASCII so that a reader can tell which character is meant, by escape or by a name in the test's title.

- [ ] The existing test for an unknown command passes unchanged.

## Parent

#26

## What to build

`tally symbols <file>` prints one report holding two counts, digits first and punctuation second, and exits 0. Today that command prints the usage line and exits 2.

For a file holding `Call 555-0199, now!`:

```
$ tally symbols note.txt
digits: 7
punctuation: 3
```

`symbols` is a report of several counts, not a count of its own: no line named `symbols` is ever printed. It is a fixed list of exactly these two counts and does not grow when `tally` learns others. The two counts are the ones `tally digits` (#31) and `tally punctuation` (#32) already print, under the same names, so the numbers always agree with those two subcommands. The file is read once per run, and both counts are taken from that one text.

#31 and #32 were built in parallel, so start by checking that they landed together cleanly: the CLI tests hold one temporary-file arrangement that both sets of tests use, and the usage line names both subcommands. If two arrangements are left, fold them into one before adding anything.

Then work in two steps:

1. Make the change easy. If the CLI's command table maps a subcommand to one count, reshape it so a subcommand names the ordered list of counts its report holds, with a list of one for each subcommand that exists. Nothing a user can see changes in this step, and every test stays green. If the table already has that shape because another effort reached `main` first, skip this step and do not reshape it again.
2. Make the easy change. Add `symbols` as the list digits, punctuation.

The report prints through the existing report formatter, which does not change. The tests reuse the temporary-file arrangement already in the CLI tests.

| Text | Report |
| --- | --- |
| (empty file) | `digits: 0` then `punctuation: 0` |
| `Call 555-0199, now!` | `digits: 7` then `punctuation: 3` |

"Symbol" does not become a glossary term. `symbols` is only the name of the subcommand that prints the two counts.

#10, #9 and #27 add `all`, `structure` and `longest`, which are also reports of several counts, to the same command table. If any of them is on `main` when you start, the same table serves it too. Each stays as its own spec decided and does not gain digits or punctuation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `tally symbols <file>` returns code 0 and a two-line report, `digits: <number>` then `punctuation: <number>`, with no trailing line break, printed through the existing report formatter.
- [ ] Both rows of the table above give the listed report, and each row runs as its own named test.
- [ ] For the same file, the two lines of the symbols report equal the line printed by `tally digits` and the line printed by `tally punctuation`, and a test checks this.
- [ ] `tally symbols` with the file left out returns code 2 and a usage line that names `digits`, `punctuation` and `symbols`. The test does not compare the whole usage line.
- [ ] `tally digits` and `tally punctuation` behave as before: their tests and the test for an unknown command pass unchanged.
- [ ] The CLI tests hold one temporary-file arrangement, used by the digits, punctuation and symbols tests alike.
- [ ] The new tests call only `run`, with the path of a temporary file, and compare the returned code and text. They do not look inside the command table and do not spawn a process.
- [ ] `npm test` passes.

## Summary

Three subcommands, two counts. A subcommand names the ordered list of counts its report holds; every count gets a subcommand of its own name, and `longest` is a fixed list of two.

```diff
 src/
 ├── cli.js         # run(argv) -> { code, out }
+├── counts.js      # each count: text -> number, no I/O

```

```diff
 run([subcommand, file])
-  count = COUNTS[subcommand]            # finds `toString` on Object.prototype
+  countNames = SUBCOMMANDS[subcommand]  # own entries only, matched exactly
   if unknown or no file -> { code: 2, out: usage }
   text = read file once, UTF-8
-  report([[subcommand, count(text)]])
+  report(countNames.map(name => [name, COUNTS[name](text)]))
```

```text
longest-word(text) = longestLength(runs of non-whitespace)
longest-line(text) = longestLength(text cut at \r\n or \n)
longestLength(pieces) = max over pieces of length in code points, 0 if none
```

## Evidence

File: `a héllo 👋👋\nbye\n`

- **Before** (`main`):

  $ tally longest-word greeting.txt
  usage: tally <count> <file>                               # exit 2
  $ tally toString greeting.txt
  toString: [object Undefined]                              # exit 0
  ```

  $ tally longest-word greeting.txt
  longest-word: 5                                           # exit 0
  $ tally longest-line greeting.txt
  longest-line: 10                                          # exit 0
  $ tally longest greeting.txt
  longest-word: 5
  longest-line: 10                                          # exit 0
  $ tally longest
  usage: tally <longest-word|longest-line|longest> <file>   # exit 2
  $ tally toString greeting.txt
  usage: tally <longest-word|longest-line|longest> <file>   # exit 2
  ```

Closes #26. Closes #31. Closes #32. Closes #33. ## Summary Three new subcommands. `digits` and `punctuation` each print a one-count report; `symbols` prints one report holding both counts, digits first. ```diff -usage: tally +usage: tally ``` A **digit** is one of `0` to `9`. A **punctuation mark** is one of the 32 ASCII punctuation characters. Nothing outside ASCII is either, and no character is both. ```diff src/ ├── cli.js # a subcommand names the ordered list of counts its report holds +├── counts.js # digits(text), punctuation(text): pure, no I/O └── report.js # unchanged ``` ```diff run([subcommand, file]) - count = COUNTS[subcommand] # one count per subcommand; the table was empty + countNames = SUBCOMMANDS[subcommand] # digits -> [digits] + # punctuation -> [punctuation] + # symbols -> [digits, punctuation] unknown subcommand or no file -> usage line, code 2 text = the file, read once as UTF-8 - formatReport([[subcommand, count(text)]]) + formatReport(countNames.map(name => [name, COUNTS[name](text)])) ``` **One change no ticket lists.** A name every object inherits, such as `constructor` or `toString`, was looked up in the command table as a known subcommand. It is now an unknown subcommand like any other (12 names, one test each). The spec's "an unknown subcommand still returns the usage line with code 2" did not hold for these on `main`, and the reshaped table would have thrown on them. ## Evidence For a file holding `Call 555-0199, now!`: - **Before** (`main`): ```text $ tally digits note.txt usage: tally (exit 2) $ tally punctuation note.txt usage: tally (exit 2) $ tally symbols note.txt usage: tally (exit 2) $ tally constructor note.txt constructor: Call 555-0199, now! (exit 0) ``` **After:** ```text $ tally digits note.txt digits: 7 (exit 0) $ tally punctuation note.txt punctuation: 3 (exit 0) $ tally symbols note.txt digits: 7 punctuation: 3 (exit 0) $ tally symbols empty.txt digits: 0 punctuation: 0 (exit 0) $ tally symbols usage: tally (exit 2) $ tally constructor note.txt usage: tally (exit 2) ``` - **Before:** `npm test`, 2 tests. **After:** `npm test`, 60 pass, 0 fail. All through `run` with a temporary file: ```text for each of the spec's 20 worked examples (text, digits, punctuation): run(['digits', file]) == { code: 0, out: 'digits: ' } run(['punctuation', file]) == { code: 0, out: 'punctuation: ' } for the empty file and 'Call 555-0199, now!': run(['symbols', file]) == { code: 0, out: 'digits: \npunctuation:

' } symbols report == the digits line, then the punctuation line each new subcommand with the file left out: code 2, usage names all three each of the 12 inherited names: code 2, usage ``` The two guard rows are there for both counts: the 32 marks each once (0, 32) and every printable ASCII character each once (10, 32). ## Merge Danger **Door:** two-way Only additions for a `tally` user: three subcommands that printed the usage line before. Reverting the merge takes them away again. **Blast Radius:** small - `spec-10-counts` and `spec-9-sentence-paragraph-counts` are not on `main` yet and touch the same four places: the command table and usage line in `src/cli.js`, `src/counts.js`, `GLOSSARY.md` and `test/cli.test.js`. Whichever merges after this one has conflicts to resolve there. The table has the same shape as on `spec-10-counts`, and the test file reuses its names (`tempFile`, `SUBCOMMANDS`), so the two join rather than compete. - A script that relied on `tally constructor ` or the like exiting 0 now gets code 2. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_0157EeLYYqTD28pMLjy1FGBE
